Works Consulted

Sources for the readings, feast data, and commemorations displayed above.

  1. Andreev, Aleksandr A. “O poryadke chteniya Evangeliya za Bozhestvennoy liturgiey v svete rekomendatsiy Pomestnogo sobora 1917–1918 gg.” Vestnik Ekaterinburgskoy dukhovnoy seminarii, no. 4(24), 2018, pp. 41–129. The rule governing how the Byzantine Gospel course's week-numbering absorbs each year's surplus or shortage (the "Lucan Jump"), used to compute the Ruthenian and Orthodox weekday/Sunday citations above. DOI: 10.24411/2224-5391-2018-10403 ↗
  2. Getcha, Archimandrite Job. The Typikon Decoded: An Explanation of Byzantine Liturgical Practice. Translated by Paul Meyendorff. St. Vladimir's Seminary Press, 2012. The book that started this project's Byzantine research: confirms the Lucan Jump date formula and the 17-week Matthean course from independent historical scholarship, documents the symmetric "Jump of the Baptism of Christ" repeat, gives the Eothinon (Resurrectional Gospel) cycle, and sets out the Degrees-of-Solemnity scale this project's own commemoration ranks are built on. svspress.com ↗
  3. Hayduk, Rev. Various Facebook comments on the mechanics of the Lucan Jump, in Byzantine Catholic discussion threads. Helped make initial sense of the Lucan Jump early in this project's research, before Getcha and Andreev's published sources were found.
  4. The Lectionary for Mass, Sunday and Weekday tables, compiled by Felix Just, S.J., Ph.D. Roman Mass citations for Ordinary Time, Lent, the Easter season, and early Advent — for 2026, Ordinary Time citations from Aug 2 onward (Weeks 18–34) come from this table's weekday-cycle data. catholic-resources.org ↗
  5. Lectionary of the Byzantine Church, Byzantine Catholic Metropolia of Pittsburgh. General plain-language background on the continuous Gospel/Epistle course and the Lucan Jump; consulted early in this project's research, superseded for the actual computation by Getcha and Andreev above. byzcath.org ↗
  6. Martyrologium Romanum (2004, editio typica altera), transcribed by Geoffrey Mondello. Source of the Roman panel's daily commemoration list; the year-round Roman Martyrology, not the smaller General Roman Calendar. bostoncatholicjournal.com ↗
  7. Menaion, per-day propers pages, Metropolitan Cantor Institute, Byzantine Catholic Archeparchy of Pittsburgh. Ruthenian fixed-feast citations and daily commemoration names. mci.archpitt.org ↗
  8. Nebesnyk, Rev. Olexiy. Personal communication. St. Anne's Byzantine Catholic Church, New Port Richey, FL. Explained how to determine the readings and hymns used on Kyriopascha (when the Annunciation coincides with Pascha), informing this project's handling of that case.
  9. Orthodox Master Menologion, Aorist Press. Cross-tradition rank data (Simple/Vigil/Great Feast, etc.) for Ruthenian and Orthodox commemorations. aoristpress.com/menologion ↗
  10. Petras, David M. (arr.). 2027 Typikon. Byzantine Seminary Press. The annual edition for ecclesiastical year September 2026–August 2027; its real, dated entries were used to confirm the Lucan Jump week-shift and other movable-cycle calculations behind the Ruthenian and Orthodox panels above.
  11. Petras, David M. (arr.). Common Typikon. Revised 2017. Byzantine Seminary Press. The Ruthenian Typikon's standardized, year-independent Formats and Commons governing precedence when a Sunday and a fixed feast concur — informs when a Great Feast suppresses the ordinary Sunday reading.
  12. Roman Lectionary/Ordo Calendars (2024–2026 editions), Roman Catholic Diocese of Saint Petersburg, FL. Roman citations for the 18 fixed-date Solemnities and Feasts; provided directly to this project by the diocese.
  13. romcal (v1.3.0), open-source liturgical calendar engine. Identifies which Roman fixed-date observances are Solemnities, Feasts, or Memorials. npmjs.com/package/romcal ↗
  14. Scripture Readings and Lives of the Saints, daily pages, Orthodox Church in America. Orthodox fixed-feast citations and daily commemoration names. oca.org/readings/daily ↗
